data.title: Product Discovery
data.tagline: The exploration process of collecting user and business evidence to validate whether a problem is real, valuable, and feasible before committing to full development.
data.learningOutcome: You can turn an idea into testable assumptions, choose low-cost behavioral evidence, and decide whether to continue, narrow, redirect, or stop.
data.description: Suppose a team wants to build a prompt-result comparison tool. Discovery turns 'creators need comparisons' into a testable assumption, then gathers evidence from recent real stories and a low-fidelity task. The evidence may support continuing, narrowing, changing direction, or stopping. Discovery reduces early uncertainty; it does not guarantee product success.

learning.assumes: You have product feature ideas but tend to treat personal intuition as universal user demand.
learning.outcome: You can turn an idea into testable assumptions, choose low-cost behavioral evidence, and decide whether to continue, narrow, redirect, or stop.

distinctions.label: PRD
distinctions.explanation: Product Discovery reduces uncertainty about the problem and solution with evidence; a PRD records the current scope, rules, and acceptance requirements. Discovery evidence can still change or stop that plan.

distinctions.label: MVP
distinctions.explanation: Product Discovery is the ongoing process of collecting evidence and changing decisions; an MVP is the smallest usable approach for testing a key assumption and may be limited to a small test group. An MVP can be one discovery experiment.

explanation.title: Before: the team treats a guess as user demand
explanation.text: The team assumes creators need prompt-result comparison and immediately asks AI to build accounts, dashboards, and settings. Shipping those features proves delivery, not that target users face the problem or would replace their current workaround.

explanation.title: Write risky assumptions, then gather behavioral evidence
explanation.text: Separate value, usability, feasibility, and business constraints. For example: creators manually compare results and this repeatedly causes rework. Reconstruct the last real event and workaround, then observe one selection task with a paper or low-fidelity prototype. Each assumption needs observable behavior; compliments alone are insufficient.

explanation.title: The outcome is a changed decision
explanation.text: If evidence supports only quick visual comparison, narrow the concept to a two-column view instead of expanding a full workspace. If the problem does not appear, pause and reassess. Continue, narrow, redirect, or stop are all valid outcomes when the evidence explains the choice.

data.boundary: Product discovery is not a meeting and has no universal sample size or method. Limited evidence only reduces uncertainty around the current assumption; new user, technical, or business evidence can reopen the decision.

lessonPractice.title: Research shows users manually compare results side by side, but they currently care only about spotting differences; nobody uses collaboration or multiple exports. What should happen next?

options.label: Narrow the scope to two-column differences and saved results, then keep observing task completion and repeat use
options.feedback: Correct. The evidence supports a smaller problem scope, so the next test should narrow the solution rather than approve every proposed feature.

options.label: Because comparison matters, finish collaboration, multiple exports, payments, and an admin dashboard together
options.feedback: Incorrect. Evidence for quick comparison does not validate the other features; expanding the scope adds untested assumptions.

options.label: Because users did not endorse the full concept, conclude that no comparison problem exists and discard the research
options.feedback: Incorrect. Users demonstrated real manual comparison behavior. Narrowing and testing again fits the evidence better.

data.agentPrompt: I want to build a prompt-result comparison tool for independent creators. Do not build the full product or high-fidelity UI yet. List the riskiest value, usability, feasibility, and business assumptions; ask what evidence already exists; then design interviews around recent real events and one low-fidelity task. Define observable signals and whether each outcome means continue, narrow, or pause.
